implementation_notes: Go's function literals are closures, so `add5 := func(y int) int { return add(5, y) }` captures the bound arguments and is the language's own answer - there is no standard-library curry because none is needed. A method value x.M is partial application spelled differently: the specification says the receiver expression is evaluated and saved when the method value is created and then used on every later call, so `handle := store.Handle` binds the receiver and leaves only the declared parameters. Idiomatic Go prefers such small explicit funcs and method values over curried chains, and when the bound data is really a group of parameters, a struct (or a struct with the method) documents it better than a nest of closures.
pitfalls: A closure shares the variable it captures: a variable declared outside the loop is one cell for all iterations (the pre-Go-1.22 `i := i` workaround), and goroutines calling the same specialisation race on that cell.
Method values keep the receiver alive, so storing them in a long-lived map pins the receiver and everything reachable from it.
A bound closure is not data: it cannot be compared (except to nil) or serialised, so it cannot be a map key or part of a config struct.
